speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINT MENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING OF VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
Under the order of introduction of
bills I had hoped to introduce to-day the bill of which notice was given yesterday, namely the Franchise Act. I regret that I am not in a position yet to do so, but I hope to do so to-morrow. Having regard to the discussion which took place in the house yesterday upon the resolution, I may say that it has been decided to appoint two enumerators in each polling subdivision for the purpose of the first enumeration. Just how these enumerators will be appointed has not been definitely decided, but the principle will be maintained of consulting the wishes or obtaining the views of the sitting member on the one hand, and of the defeated candidate on the other hand, and where there was more than one defeated candidate, of the one who had the highest number of votes.
On the other clause, in regard to appeals from the decision of the revising officer, it has been decided that there shall be an appeal to the county or district judge in those provinces which have county and district judges, but as all provinces are not alike in respect to their judicial conveniences some difficulty has been experienced in drafting a suitable clause. When the bill comes before the house I may have to ask the assistance of some of the legal members from the various provinces in regard to difficulties which might arise. The principle in that case will be to limit the time as far as possible and to simplify the proceedings by way of appeal and make them informal and expeditious. I hope to bring down the bill for presentation to the house to-morrow or it may be Monday.

speechtext: The assurance which the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) has just given will meet I am sure-as he has seen-with the general approval of the house. Might I inquire, seeing that the bill is not yet finally printed, whether the government has included a clause which will oblige revising officers to notify the electors as to where they are to vote? If not, would the government take into consideration including such an obligation? I believe official notification to electors is something which would avoid much in the way of expense to candidates and would really constitute a substantial improvement.

subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINT MENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING OF VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: They do it in cities.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINT MENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING OF VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: I think the suggestion is worth considering, but the expense would be very considerable if every elector on the voters' list has to be notified where he votes. It has never been the custom heretofore. All I can say is that I shall bring the suggestion before my colleagues.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINT MENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING OF VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext:
If I might just add this word-I know a discussion is not in order. Viewing the matter in its true light, elections are a necessary part of the machinery of government, and for that reason it seems to me the state itself should meet any legitimate unavoidable expenses incidental to securing a complete and fair election; that expenses incidental to a necessary service to the voter should not be made an obligation on those who may be nominated as candidates. Unless a provision of that kind is in-

Questions

eluded those who may become candidates or their supporters will have to bear the expenses of notifying electors where they are to vote. With lists prepared by the state official, notification of the place of voting is something which really ought to be regarded as also a part of the necessary expenses of elections.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINT MENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING OF VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: There is another practical difficulty. The revising officer would not be in a position to notify the people more than as to the subdivision in which their names are registered, because until the writ of election is issued and returning officers appointed no one knows where the polling places will be.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ELECTORAL FRANCHISE-APPOINT MENT OF FRANCHISE COMMISSIONER-PRINTING OF VOTERS' LISTS
speechtext: Some arrangement could be worked out, whereby this obligation might be made a duty of either the revising officers or the returning officers. With the franking of notices, the expenses ought to be comparatively little.

Twelve or fourteen years ago I built a steel vessel in New Glasgow which I operated for some time. Later I sold her while she was lying in Boston through a broker, a former Nova Scotian, who conducted a ship brokerage business there for many years. I went to the custom house in Pictou, saw the registrar of shipping, and made the usual declaration of change of ownership. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On section 568-Certificates cancelled or suspended in other parts of His Majesty's dominions.

Mr. Chairman, does this not seem to be a hardship? It would appear from the section that a Canadian who is a master could have his certificate cancelled or suspended by reason of an investigation in another dominion. A few moments ago the minister, replying to the hon. member for New Westminster, stated that he did not know whether Great Britain would recognize a suspension or cancellation from a court or commission in Canada. By section 568 the minister will adopt a cancellation or suspension which would arise, by reason of an investigation in another part of the British commonwealth. In my view that arrangement is hard on Canadians.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The hon. member will notice that the provision is not imperative. The section states that-
The minister may adopt and carry out said cancellation.
That means that if after having examined and studied the record and the judgment rendered by the court outside of Canada the minister is convinced that a proper judgment was rendered, he may maintain the cancellation of the certificate.
But it would still be a court in another country which would suspend or cancel the certificate of a Canadian citizen.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: No.
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: No, it means that the final judgment as to the effect of the cancellation in Canada will be rendered by the minister, after having studied the whole proceeding. Surely if he thinks that the proceeding was not fair or the judgment has not dealt fairly with the mariner, the minister would not be bound to maintain the cancellation.
Some ministers do not enjoy the confidence of everybody.
This is a new section; where did the idea come from?
It is imperialism.
Where did the request for the new section come from? This clause was never in any of our shipping legislation.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: There is no mention in the bill as drafted, but I think it comes under the imperial agreements.
I thought so. Is there reciprocity?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: My hon. friends will find the provision at page 7 of the British Commonwealth Merchant Shipping Agreement.
Please read it.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
It reads:
The court on formal investigation shall be empowered to cancel or suspend a certificate of competency or services granted by the administration of another part of the commonwealth only as to affect its validity within the jurisdiction of the part in which investigation is held, but the administration by which the certificate was granted may adopt such cancellation or suspension.
It is not the same.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I contend it is absolutely fair.
No, it is not.
It is not the same, at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Upon the return of a Canadian mariner who while abroad was guilty of certain offences meriting cancellation or suspension of his certificate when on a British ship in another part of the commonwealth, the minister will look info the record and conduct a review of what took place abroad. If he finds that the judgment was justified I see no objection to his maintaining the cancellation or suspension.

I have no objection to that, provided the arrangement is reciprocal, and the same treatment is given in another British country to a Britisher whose certificate has been cancelled here. But the paragraph the minister read from the convention does not agree with the section now under consideration, and there is no reciprocal provision.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: If my hon. friend would read the agreement he would find it is reciprocal; it must be.
But the agreement is in force only when legislation is adopted in the various dominions.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Of course.

It is adopted when legislation is accepted to ratify or to give effect to it, and it may be given effect to under certain conditions. In the present instance the only condition is that the minister may or may not suspend or ratify a suspension or cancellation, and I say that very little safeguard is provided.

Canada Shipping Act

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The imperial agreement is to the effect that every part of the British Empire should adopt the same legislation or legislation along the same lines.
Why not indicate that arrangement in the statute?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: That is the agreement. If other parts of the empire do not follow the agreement, surely we will do otherwise; the government would not give effect to the section or would come to the house for a change in our law. At the present time we are taking the lead, being the greater dominion, and are adopting the legislation based on the imperial agreement. We expect that all the other parts of the empire will follow.

Is there anything in the bill which, for instance, gives power to a Canadian court to cancel for misdemeanour the certificate of a captain coming from England on an English ship? Is there anything giving any court in Canada the power to cancel the certificate of such a man for misdemeanour on the high seas, accident, or for any other reason? I can see nothing. If there is no such provision we have no right to have the section before us in our statutes.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Section 562 covers the point the hon. member has raised. It is as follows:
Any court holding a formal investigation pursuant to this part of this act may cancel or suspend a certificate of competency or service granted by another part of His Majesty's dominions so far only as concerns its validity within Canada.
That is it exactly-"within Canada."

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
Other parts of the
empire have no greater power with respect to our mariner's certificate.

If it is cancelled in England, the validity under this legislation is null and void, even in Canadian waters, until the Canadian minister has made an investigation. The section states that the Canadian minister "may" maintain the cancellation. Therefore if he does not maintain the cancellation it should not take effect. But he has power to maintain or not to maintain the cancellation, as he sees fit, and no such provision exists in the British act.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
My hon. friend will
readily understand that so long as the minister has not maintained the cancellation abroad, the certificate of the mariner is in force in Canada, and the judgment or finding of the court abroad has no effect in Canada.
It is left to the minister to decide whether or not he should maintain the cancellation in Canada, and exactly the same kind of legislation is supposed to be adopted by other parts of the empire.

If they do not adopt it,
will the minister change this section?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: In connection with this reciprocal arrangement the same law should be adopted by every part of the empire.

But it would be so
easy for the government to insert the words: "provided the certificate has been cancelled or suspended in a part of the British dominions which has adopted a similar provision." That w'ould be very easy to do.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
I think there is some protection in the last section of the bill. It is as follows:
This act shall not come into force until a date to be fixed by proclamation of the governor in council published in the Canada Gazette: Provided that he may, in the same manner and from time to time, bring any portion or portions only of this act into force.
If some parts of this legislation are not enacted in other parts of the empire we may never proclaim them.
There are 719 sections; surely there will not be 719 proclamations.

Suppose the captain of a
British ship operating in Canada came before the court, so long as that vessel was operating in Canadian waters would we have full jurisdiction to cancel the certificates of the captain, mates or engineers?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Yes.

Yes, we have, so far as
Canada is concerned.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Section agreed to.

I want to revert to section 562. We are rushing through these sections * so fast that we are having no opportunity to read them, let alone give them any consideration. In section 562 we are abrogating our rights in regard to our certificates to our own captains and leaving those rights to a court in some point other than the dominion. Then we come to section 568, a new section, and we find there again that the certificates of Canadian captains may be cancelled by a foreign court, and we adopt the section without giving our own captains a hearing. I submit that is not god citizen-
Canada Shipping Act

ship or good Canadianism. Then, although we have not yet reached clause 570, may I say that it reads as follows:
The minister shall not order a rehearing in Canada in connection with a shipping casualty in respect of *which a formal investigation has been held in another part of His Majesty's dominions.
I say that that section should read absolutely the other way, and should say, "may order" instead of "shall not order."

The hon. member for Pictou is quite right. Under section 569 the minister may order the rehearing of an investigation which has been held in Canada, if there is new evidence, or if for any reason he believes there has been a miscarriage of justice. But when the cancellation or suspension has been the result of an investigation in another country, under section 570 the minister shall not order a rehearing in Canada in connection with a shipping casualty in respect of which a formal investigation has been held in another part of His Majesty's dominions. That is a discrimination not only against Canadians but against Canadian courts and Canadian investigations, and the minister will be powerless when there has been an investigation outside of Canada. When it is a Canadian investigation he has the power of ordering a rehearing. Surely my hon. friend from Pictou is right. These are provisions which seem absolutely uncalled for.

I am not content to
allow a Nova Scotia captain who has sailed all over the world to be demoted by somebody in Hongkong or Ireland or some other part of the world. The minister should not abrogate his rights in that way.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: The minister does not abrogate his rights because there is one thing he can do, and that is to ignore the judgment of an external court.

Surely we are masters
in our own house.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
The minister has only one thing to do, and that is to ignore the judgment and then the certificate is still valid in Canada.
Section 570 to which the ex-Minister of Justice referred is a new section. I understand that it also is a provision in the British commonwealth agreement of 1931, and the reason probably is that when a misdemeanour has been committed outside of Canada it is very difficult to have a rehearing in this country because the witnesses are far away and an inquiry would be very expensive.
[Mr. Cantley.l
It goes beyond a misdemeanour.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: I want to remind my hon. friends that the provision is absolutely reciprocal, being part of an agreement arrived at by all the different parts of the empire.

But it will be reciprocal
only when similar legislation is enacted by the other parliaments, and I am doubtful whether Australia, for instance, will enact legislation giving to a court in Canada the right to cancel Australian certificates, because Australia is pretty jealous of her rights.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext: Australia was represented at that conference.

But the legislation has
not gone through the Australian parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
It is well understood,
and it was so stated when the bill was introduced, that Canada is the first of the dominions to enact the provisions agreed upon in the conventions. The intention of this government is to put in force reciprocal agreements only when the other parts of the empire have adopted similar legislation. If they do not do so we shall see that our law is changed. But in this bill we are setting an example and inducing the other parts of the empire to adopt the same legislation. They have already agreed to do it. The conventions have been duly signed by the representatives of all the dominions.

I know, but parliament
is master in each of those countries.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
If we do not accept
section 568 or section 570 we are setting aside the convention that was accepted by Canada and the other parts of the empire.
The other parts of the empire have not adopted any of this as yet.

speechtext: But we have agreed to pass this legislation and the other dominions are waiting for this legislation in order to follow.
If the minister agreed to do that 'he did something he had no right to do. Parliament has the last word as far as we are concerned.

speechtext: I did not agree myself; the representatives of Canada agreed.

The proceedings this afternoon and evening have been somewhat monotonous, with only an occasional interruption from the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid).

Oh, Mr. Chairman, I rise to a
point of order.

I cannot allow this clause
to pass without calling attention to it. It deals with coastal shipping and is of special interest to us who live on the prairies because it is intended to affect-
Prairie schooners.

-shipping on the great
lakes. The course of the government in this matter has been rather peculiar. It has been devious; we would really like to know what the government intends to do. Two years ago the government brought in a bill-I think it got as far as first reading and was then withdrawn ; at any rate was not proceeded with- the intention of which was to give to Canadian vessels the monopoly of carrying Canadian grain on the great lakes. They probably thought it wise at the time to withdraw that bill, but last year they tried another tack. In the Bill J that was brought in last year they tried to put it across by a few changes in the definitions. The coasting trade of Canada was defined thus:
"Coasting trade of Canada" means the transportation by water or by land and water of goods or passengers from one place in Canada to the same or another place in Canada, whether or not such transportation is direct or via a foreign port outside of Canada and includes any part of such transportation.
The last part of that definition was added in order to take care of the particular situation that the government wanted to bring about. In section 932 of the Canada Shipping Act the coasting trade of Canada was defined as including:
-the carriage by water of goods or passengers from one port or place in Canada to another port or place in Canada.
Attention was drawn to that matter, and then the government decided to bring about the desired end by another method. So a bill was brought in last year restoring the old definition of coasting trade, making the change in what would correspond to section 663 of this act, which says:
No goods shall be transported by_ water or by land and water, from one place in Canada
Canada Shipping Act

to another place in Canada, either directly or by way of foreign port, or for any part of the transportation in any ship other than a British ship.
That bill passed the house in face of opposition from this side, with the support of hon. members from the west representing farming constituencies who managed to convince themselves, or at least who seemed to convince themselves, that there was no danger to the grain interests in this clause. That bill passed the house, but it was not proclaimed by the government, and again we wonder what the real intention of the government is in this matter.
These particular sections form a part of the bill now before us. I do not suppose there is any use in continuing to debate this matter at any length, but I should like to repeat in a general way the objections we from the west take to this clause. Everyone knows that for the last two or three years the price of wheat has been at the lowest point in history, though it is not quite so low as it was a year or two ago. A great deal has been said in the past month or so with regard to relieving the burdens of the farmers. The famous marketing act ostensibly was devised with that purpose in view. It seems to me a much more sensible procedure would have been to consider some of the other difficulties the farmer has to meet. In my judgment it would have been much more sensible to reduce the cost of production, which could be done in a number of ways. It might be done by modifying the high protective measures that have been placed against some of the things used by the farmer, such as the ten per cent duty on barbed wire, the twenty-five per cent duty on cream separators and the twenty-five per cent duty that now applies to practically all lines of farm machinery, whereas previously the duty ranged from six to ten or twelve per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
What section is the hon.
member discussing?

I am discussing this bill
as it affects the farmer, and I am indicating that since it is essential that production costs should be lowered this is one of the ways in which the government might approach the matter. However, I quite understand that hon. members opposite, especially those representing farming districts in the west, do not like to have these things brought to their attention. As we see it this bill is calculated to put the carrying of grain on the great lakes into the hands of a Canadian monopoly. As

we see it, it is essential that we should preserve what we have at present, that is, Buffalo as a strategic point at which to have wheat placed, whence it can be carried either via Montreal-and a great deal does go that way -or via New York. It means a great deal to the shipment of wheat to have a choice of routes, and we consider anything that will jeopardize the Shipment of grain via that route to be a menace to the well being of the farmers.
It may be very interesting to note that wheat that has gone by that route sometimes has brought a higher price than wheat that has gone via the Canadian route. I took some interest in this matter, and shortly after coming down here at the beginning of this session I wrote the bureau of statistics to find out how much wheat had gone via the United States route and how much had gone via Canadian ports since the Ottawa agreements came into effect. The bureau of statistics gave me more information than I asked for, and here is what I find. The figures are given month by month from November, 1932, to December, 1933, with the price received for the grain in each month. The totals are as follows: Shipped via Canadian sea and river ports, 104,917,854 bushels; via United States ports, 50,883,301 bushels. The amount of money received for the grain shipped via Canadian ports was $62,428,715, and the amount received for wheat shipped via United States ports was $31,396,715. I was interested to see just what that would amount to per bushel. To my amazement I found that the wheat shipped via United States ports brought 61-7 cents per bushel, while the wheat shipped via Canadian ports brought only 59-5 cents per bushel. I could not understand those figures, and I wrote the bureau again to find out just at what point the price of wheat was fixed. In reply I had this letter:
I have your letter of the 12th instant with reference to the memorandum mailed you on the second respecting Canada's exports of wheat to the United Kingdom via Canadian sea and river ports, and via the United States.
As regards the value, I wish to point out that the value of exports of Canadian merchandise is the actual cost or the value at the time of exportation at the points in Canada whence originally shipped.
In my second letter to the bureau I had stated that I was anxious to know if we could possibly arrive at it what effect the six cent preference had on wheat shipped via United States ports. In that regard, in the same letter they said:
We have no record as to the amount of wheat going via American ports that receive

Canada Shipping Act
the benefit of the preference. With reference to the diversion of wheat shipped to the United Kingdom via the United States, I wish to advise that according to United States in transit figures, a very large percentage of Canadian wheat shown in Canadian trade statistics as exported to the United Kingdom via the United States border ports, is diverted while in transit via the United States, to other destinations, chiefly the continent of Europe. The percentage varies from year to year. For the calendar year, 1931, however, of the total amount of Canadian wheat shipped via United States Atlantic ports, about 27 per cent was destined for the United Kingdom, and in 1932, 17 per cent. There are no statistics available as yet for the year 1933. Then, again, it must be remembered that a considerable amount of Canadian wheat exported to overseas countries via the United States is rerouted from United States lake ports for shipment via Canadian ports chiefly the port of Montreal. For the calendar year 1933 the amount of rerouted wheat from United States lake ports for shipment via Canadian ports, amounted to 4,915,433 bushels.
So that while that figure is of a considerable size, the fact remains that the great bulk of the wheat recorded as having been shipped via American ports actually went that way. The point to which I wish to call the attention of hon. members is this: I am not able to explain-and if any hon. member can, I should like him to do so-why it is that the wheat we shipped to the United Kingdom via American ports brought us a higher price than the wheat shipped via Canadian ports. While I cannot explain that, there is one point which does seem perfectly clear, and that is that the six cent preference we were supposed to get on our wheat is not worth the snap of a finger.
And never was.
Would we be better off without the preference?
If anyone can give any other explanation for it I will give him the opportunity to do so.
Would we be better off without the preference?
Just another piece of humbug.

I do not say we would be better off without it, but we are certainly no better off with it. That is the situation, despite the fact that we heard a lot of talk about a sheltered market for a large proportion of our wheat.
Would you vote against a preference?
I think the hon. member had better discuss subjects he knows something about.
I do know something about it.

I wish to protest against this section of the shipping bill, although I have not the slightest expectation that my protests will in any measure be effective. I am speaking for the farmers of the prairie provinces to whom the cheapest possible rates for the shipment of their wheat are absolutely essential. Even half a cent per bushel may mean a great deal to them, and on their behalf I wish to protest, as I did last year, against the enactment of this section. I therefore move:
That subsection 1 of section 663 be amended' by striking therefrom the words, "either directly or by way of a foreign port, or for any part of the transportation."

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the hon. member (Mr. Brown) has quoted from a communication he received from the bureau of statistics in which, if I caught his reading of it correctly, he indicated that for the 50,000.000 bushels of wheat exported from Canada via American ports the return indicated 01 cents a bushel, while for the 104,000,000 bushels exported from Canada via Canadian ports the return indicated 59 cents a bushel. That I think was in round figures his observation, and he deduced from that the conclusion that it is in the interest of the western wheat grower to export his wheat from Canada via American ports. He has asked, and I think quite properly, if there is any explanation for the difference in those figures. I think I can indicate to him, and to anyone who will give the matter careful and impartial thought, certain factors that enter into the situation. It is I think not difficult to explain.
In the first place, it will be noted that the point of shipment there recorded is in all probability Port Arthur or Fort William. I have similar figures in the report of the board of grain commissioners but covering a different period of time, so they do not synchronize exactly with the figures quoted. The point of departure, however, is Port Arthur or Fort William. Apparently we have no record in the figures given of what the grade of wheat was. It is obvious that grade No. 1, for instance, would bring a much higher price than grades 2, 3 or 4. I think perhaps the major portion of the wheat so exported would be grade No. 2. The first factor is the grade of the wheat, and there is no record of the precise quantity of the various grades that
Canada Shipping Act

were included in those two different parcels.
The second point I would indicate is this, that not only is there a difference in grade, but the shipments cover the whole period of the year. The wheat exported from United States ports, for instance, might have been shipped largely during a certain period and not so much during another period, or the period and quantity may have varied; and as the price of wheat varies from day to day and week to week-we had some very sharp fluctuations last year, particularly last summer, in the middle of the calendar year-here again you have not a constant factor but a varying factor.
The third point I would suggest to my hon. friend, and this is perhaps the main cause of it, is that Europe, due to the very high protection it has had against incoming wheat from any part of the world and the stimulation given to the production of soft wheat in its own territory, is buying very largely No. 1 grade in order to get the strongest wheat for mixing purposes with their flour. Therefore it is reasonable to assume that the largest portion of the export of No. 1 wheat went to European ports and not to British ports. I think with these three factors in mind it is not hard to understand the variation in the price of wheat as coming from those two different sources. But in any case one could not possibly base a definite argument or conclusion upon the result obtained merely by dividing the quantity of wheat into the total amount received therefor.
If I may interrupt for a moment, is it reasonable to suppose that all the better grades of grain would be shipped through American ports?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce

speechtext: I had a recollection that after our first legislation was enacted the rates were increased on the lakes.

The point I am making is that there is an abundance of shipping on the great lakes.
As far as our American neighbours are concerned, Canadian vessels cannot go over there and carry grain or other cargoes in the same way that American vessels have been permitted in part to do on this side, and all that this legislation is doing is to synchronize our legislation with that of the United States, and giving to the Canadian carrier the opportunity of carrying the goods for Canadian ports, while still preserving to the exporter of the west the right to ship his grain to Buffalo or any other American port he wishes by American bottoms or Canadian bottoms. So I think there is no danger to the exporter of a lack of competition or of any penalizing of the farmer by way of an increased rate.

Quite so. While I am on my feet I should like to refer to sections 4 and 5 of the Inland Water Freight Rates Act. This act contains special provisions with

speechtext: I am glad my hon. friend has asked that question. I do not think there is any danger of that 'happening. One reason is that which I have indicated already, the surplus of shipping. In addition, there are those sections of the act to which my hon. friend referred and which were not at the moment in my mind. The administration of the Inland Water Freight Rates Act is under the board of grain commissioners and, of course, myself as minister. That act gives a very definite control. This control was exercised over two years ago when the Canadian and American shipping raised the rate for a short time to seven and a half cents. The board of grain commissioners keep a constant watch on the situation, and should any occasion arise, that control can be exercised. This matter does not pass out of the control of the government, even when parliament is not sitting. When parliament is sitting, of [DOT] course we can deal with it in parliament if it is so desired. that this question was discussed at some length last year when this provision and some others were brought in by way of special legislation which, however, has never become law owing to the fact that it has not been proclaimed. Now we are again confronted with exactly the same situation.

In a

' Mr. SPEAKMAN: That phase of the matter was not -made at all clear last year; the impression was left that once grain had been shipped to Buffalo in a United States vessel it would foe impossible for it to be shipped in any vessel back to a Canadian port. To my mind there is no value in any further discussion of this matter, to consider freight rates of past years because it must be pointed out that during all these years and up to the present United States competition has been in force and such freight rates are no criterion as to possible rates where competition is eliminated as this legislation has not so far been put into force.
It will be the maximum.

Freight rates on the
great lakes have also been a determining factor so far as rates from Vancouver and other points are concerned, because it has always been pointed out that wheat at least, being a commodity international in its character and where every fraction of a cent of additional cost must be paid by the producer who ships the grain, will naturally follow the cheapest route, whether western or eastern, whether to Buffalo, Port Colborne, Montreal or any other port; and the cheapest route will set the price very largely for all the other routes by which grain is shipped. Wheat is also in a singular position in this respect, perhaps beyond all other commodities, that every fraction of a cent of additional cost in the handling and shipment is reflected at once in a reduction in price to the producer. The price is set in Liverpool or the markets of the world. Every fraction of a cent which it costs to carry it to that market is taken from the amount which the producer receives. So the route by which and the conditions under which his grain is shipped are of direct and vital interest to the producer of wheat. Frankly, may I say, we look with some trepidation upon any action or act which removes any competitive factor in the transportation of our wheat. We are not inclined to trust too much to statutory protection, to the powers of the grain commission to regulate, or any other form of control, because however effective that control may be, we know that one of the most effective forms of control, and one which under this act will be

Canada Shipping Act
removed in some degree at least, is that which comes into operation through competition of other means of transportation. The slightest restriction or limitation of that competition may be-I do not say necessarily will be-may be reflected in the price that the farmer receives. And may I say that under present conditions, or under any conditions, the manifest duty of those whose interest- for this we have sometimes been accused, and we accept the accusation-whose interest is primarily although not soLely that of the farmer producer, is to make certain to the best of their ability that no additional costs are placed on the transport of that commodity, and that no controlling factor is removed and no injustice done. It is not that the western farmer would not prefer, the cost and other things being equal, to have his grain carried in Canadian bottoms. He would. But he cannot afford to pay for that sentiment, and he cannot afford to take the chance of an increase in cost through the removal of that controlling factor. We know quite well that owing to the composition of the house and for other reasons our protest can be only a protest, but we make it in the hope that being seized of the situation, and in view of the forebodings with which the farmer views this bill, the government will see to it that by every statutory power at their disposal, under section 165 and Other sections, under the Inland Water Freight Rates Act and other acts, every means will be taken when this competitive protection is removed to see that the farmer and producer does not suffer.
I shall not waste the time of the committee in dealing further with this matter, but I desire to associate myself with those to my right who have already given voice to the views of the western farmers in stating our doubt, our trepidation with regard to this part of the bill, which, no matter what may be said, no matter what other regulations may be in force, no matter what other powers of control may be at hand, does remove one of the most effective factors in the control of the transportation cost of wheat and therefore of the price which we may receive.

The question raised by
the 'hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) in submitting an amendment to this clause has been emphasized by the hon. member who has just resumed his seat (Mr. Speakman). The broad question which has been indirectly raised is that of the routing and transportation of western grain. These hon. gentlemen claim that they cannot afford to pay for sentiment. I submit that there is a part of this country 74726-253
and a class of people in this country who have been paying for sentiment for a long time, and have not yet complained. This amendment raises the question of the routing and transportation of grain and indirectly the question of trans-Canada transportation, and the use of Canadian ports either on the Atlantic or on the Pacific. I submit that the people of the west should now begin to think of paying a little for sentiment in this country. We in the maritimes are paying for sentiment. We have been supporting the west; the millions of dollars which have been furnished to the west in the last three or four years-
Order.

-that have been guaranteed are contributed to by the east for sentiment. If these western farmers and wheat growers would think for a moment of what the people of the east have to pay to maintain the transportation systems, both rail and water, they would I believe be satisfied to pay at least half a cent or a cent a bushel more for transporting their wheat by an allCanadian route, either by water or by rail. I cannot subscribe to this amendment, Mr. Chairman, and if it were possible to make the section a little stronger, to make it an absolute prohibition so that western people could not ship grain by any other than Canadian ports and Canadian railways or ships, I think we would serve the country well.

There is
a Canada first policy.

A few evenings ago I
heard the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) make some such statement as that of the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Michaud), and I took it upon myself that night to tell the Prime Minister-and he did not need telling-just what contribution the west has made to eastern Canada. If hon. members are going to talk now of our paying for sentiment, let me say that we have done nothing else ever since we have been in the west. Take the tariff, for instance; on everything we have to buy it is tariff, tariff, tariff. My hon. friend talks about paying for sentiment. I object, Mr. Chairman; I do not care who says it, whether it comes from this side of the house or the other or any corner of the house, as long as I am able to stand on my feet I propose to say that that is not true, and that the west is not prepared to pay any more for sentiment than we have

Canada Shipping Act

already paid. There is no sentiment in this. My hon. friend asks: Why don't you compel all Canadian wheat to go through Canadian ports?

The best
way.

Yes, but suppose the
United States government said that any wheat going into Buffalo could not be carried out of Buffalo in a Canadian bottom, what action could the government take?

Wait and
see.

Would you. take the
action that is now suggested? Do you see what you are starting?

Address
the Chair.

The Chair would not
reply, I am addressing the minister through the chair, as I would like to have a reply. We are now taking a stand to prevent American bottoms from taking wheat from Buffalo to the port of Montreal or any other Canadian port. Suppose the United States should say to us: You shall not take any wheat, either American or Canadian, from the port of Buffalo to anywhere. What action would you take?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The suggestion my hon. friend makes is of course a complete violation of aJll known international shipping practice. It is recognized that coastwise trade is the business of a country, but it is also recognized that the movement of goods out of one country's port to another country's port is open shipping. Of course any country could take the stand that no shipping from another country should enter its ports, but that would be a complete violation of international amity in regard to transportation.
Let me ask one question. Is wheat the only commodity that is shipped to United States ports that cannot be shipped back to Canada in United States bottoms?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Certainly not. The only reason wheat comes into the question is because wheat happens to be the major cargo in this case. That applies to anything you like to mention, oats, barley or anything else. There is no coal moving and I suppose there are not many other cargoes, but if there were it would apply to them as well.
So that when we come down to it the western grain grower is the one who has to pay through the nose in the application of this act.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Not at all.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. gentleman opposite who spoke last said there was no sentiment in this matter. There is no doubt of that so far as he is concerned, but if you want to see an exhibition of pure selfishness I commend you to the speech of the reverend gentleman from Ldsgar (Mr. Brown). For ten years I listened to hon. gentlemen opposite, when they were in power, bellyaching about the Hudson bay railway, and finally we spent $60,000,000 to build that railway and grain storage elevators there. Why don't they use them? Why are they coming here to-day wanting to send grain through United States ports? Have our ship owners on the great lakes no rights? Are they not Canadians and entitled to some consideration? Then hon. gentlemen opposite spoke of what we have done for the west, as though we had no right to mention it at all. Why, we have given the west $30,000,000, $40,000,000 or $50,000,000 in the last two or three years to relieve the situation there. Apparently that counts for nothing at all. Now the hon. member for Lisgar comes along; he will not employ a Canadian vessel at all. We must send all our grain through United States ports, and he deludes himself with the idea that he gets a better price by sending it that way than by sending it through Canadian ports. He cannot prove it; indeed there is no foundation whatever for that suggestion. If the hon. gentleman had his way all the ships that have been built on the great lakes, largely to relieve the situation of which he complains, ships which are now lying idle in the St. Lawrence river by the score, would be wiped out.. Then he would find, before he was very much older, that when the Americans had complete control they would make him pay through the nose for every bushel of wheat they carried for him and his western friends, and possibly they would ultimately force the bulk of it to be sent through that more or less impossible channel that cost $60,600,000 to construct.
I am sorry this question has been raised as between east and west.
Perhaps you are, but you raised it.

I am sorry my hon. friend who is a new member of the house has discussed the question which has been threshed

Canada Shipping Act
out here again and again; evidently as yet he has only the maritime point of view. In general terms I should like to say that whatever the east has done for the west has been repaid over and over and over again.
How?
It has been repaid over and over again.
We have only your unsupported testimony on that point.

The billions of bushels of grain that have been raised in the west during the last thirty years have kept alive the industries of eastern Canada. But for that there would have been no industries in eastern Canada. I do not want to discuss this matter further; I a,m sorry that it has been introduced. There was no occasion for it.
It was you who introduced it.

No; all I asked was that the routes we already have should be maintained, because the western farmer is not in a position to even run the risk of having to pay higher freight rates than he is paying at the present time. That is all we are asking in this amendment.
Mr. MaeMILLAN (Saskatoon): This is purely a political speech of the hon. member.

It is nothing of the kind.
Mr. MaeMILLAN (Saskatoon): There is not one word in this act that will make the western farmers pay one cent more for freight on their grain. You are just saying this sort of thing for the benefit of the Liberal press in western Canada.

I object to the statement made by the hon. member for Saskatoon. We have threshed this thing out on the floor of this house year after year ever since it was first suggested, not only when there was an election in the province of Saskatchewan. I should like to ask hon. members from that province and from all the western provinces who are sitting behind the government whether they are in agreement with regard to this clause. If this thing goes through and is put into operation you will have the maximum freight rate on the great lakes at all times, and you will eliminate one-third of the competition there to-day.

Yes, you will. You are not going to prevent an Aim'erican bottom from going to the head of the lakes and returning to Buffalo, but you are going to prevent it from going from Buffalo back to any Canadian port. In many years fifty per cent of the Canadian wheat goes through Buffalo.
Too much.

Probably it is. It goes
that way not because of sentiment but because of economics.
Mr. MaeMILLAN (Saskatoon): Fifty per cent went via New York in the years you are talking about.

No, it did not. There is no place on the American continent where Canadian, wheat can be assembled so readily as it can be done at Buffalo. All that is necessary to prove that statement is to look at the great expenditures that Canadians have made at Buffalo in order to take advantage of the routes out of that port.
Who made the expenditure? The grain growers themselves did.

We did; there is not a dollar of government money invested in Buffalo t.o-day. It is the money of the Canadian growers, paid through the nose to the grain trade.
Mr. MaeMILLAN (Saskatoon): The wheat pool.

Yes, and the grain
growers' company and many of the other interests in Winnipeg. The minister said the lowest rate we ever had was the rate of two and three-quarters cents per bushel this year. If you eliminate this competition we are going to be subjected to the maximum rate.

As one coming from the province of Saskatchewan I want to dissent from what has been said. In the view of some hon. gentlemen Buffalo may be the cheapest and best place to assemble wheat from western Canada, but I would remind hon. members that hundreds of millions of bushels of Canadian wheat are passing to the British market through the ports of Vancouver and Churchill. This is an entirely new situation which has come into existence in the last two years. Evidently my hon. friend does not know what is happening in Canada. He just sees the country from the point of view of his own constituency, nothing more. When my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) was speaking he said all the west was subject to these rates from Fort
Canada Shipping Act

William. I venture to say that half the grain from his own district goes to the market through Vancouver, and it will continue to go in that way. Then so long as we have that competition between two of our own ports, which we have paid for and which are supported by us, what on earth is the good of talking about raising rates somewhere else? Last summer they lowered rates in order to kill Churchill, and they succeeded. Let them raise the rates, if they dare, and they will build up Churchill. Go to it. It will prevent Churchill from being destroyed, and will save for the western farmer the best port in Canada. If the eastern Canadians do not like to meet our competition, they will have to take the consequences, that is all. I am not afraid of eastern Canadian competition, or competition on the great lakes. We will build up our own trade in our own way, as we have been doing it in the last two years. If the hon. member for South Battleford wishes to laugh about it, he may do so, but we are going to build up trade in that way. I have every sympathy with eastern Canada, because, thank God, I was born in the east. But I live in the west; we have to meet western conditions, and they may as well make up their minds to do so because we are not going to be defeated in our efforts to build up the trade of that country.

The last speaker indicated it would be a good thing by law to force all Canadian grain through Canadian ports. Suppose the Americans did that, what would become of Canadian grain going through the port of Montreal?

The last speaker from the province of Saskatchewan has reminded me that the grain from my constituency and that of the greater part of Alberta goes through the port of Vancouver, and not across the great lakes. I am aware of that fact. But I am aware of this fact, too, that the rates on any one of these routes is a factor in setting the rates for any one of the others, and that the rates through Vancouver are at least partially set by the competition supplied by the great lakes, by Churchill, by rail to Montreal, and every other route. It is a matter of balance and competition between one point and another, and no one point can hold itself independent of the conditions at the other point. The rates are set in that way.
Mr. COWAN (Long Lake); Precisely.

May I suggest to the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. MacMillan) for whom I have great personal regard, that

this is not a political question, nor, so far as I am concerned, is it raised as a matter of political policy or political advantage for the Liberal press. If my hon. friend would listen to my friends sitting to my right I think he would readily appreciate at least this fact, that I am not persona grata with the Liberal party or supporting Liberal members at the present time, just as I was certainly not persona grata with the Conservative party when the Liberal party was in power. At that time I was accused of being a Liberal, because I cooperated with the only party in parliament competent to do anything. Now I am accused of being a Conservative, because I cooperate, again, with the only party in parliament competent to do anything. I will cooperate with any government prepared to do anything in Canada's interests, so that no one can accuse me of being for the Liberal party. I am, however, speaking from the point of view which is not only my own but that of the majority of the people whom I represent and who, as has been suggested, ship via the port of Vancouver but are vitally affected by everything which takes place, and by every competitive or non-competitive factor. We are dependent upon and subject to the influence of what takes place at every other point, and I do suggest that one of the most potent factors in regulating the cost of transporting our Canadian wheat has been the competition by American bottoms on the great lakes. I deplore that fact. I deplore the fact that at times during the past years Canadian bottoms have not seen fit to give greater competition. May I point out also that I fully appreciate and understand the policy of the government, namely that within the confines of Canada, and to the degree to which the government of Canada is competent to effect that end, the different ports of Canada shall each be given an advantage within Canada. And as each is given an advantage it is the desire of the government that all will be on a parity, and on a higher parity than would otherwise exist. I understand that. But I understand this also, that perhaps beyond any other commodity in Canada wheat is purely and completely international in its Character. It cannot be controlled by any purely Canadian action. It is predominantly sold on the world market, and the domestic price is a subsidiary factor dependent entirely upon the world market. Again differing from any other article, every fraction of cost in removing wheat from the producer to the ultimate market in the old world is deducted from the price received by the producer. It stands in a class by itself.

Canada Ship-ping Act
It cannot be benefited and it may be injured by any purely national action in respect to it. That is why I suggest that the government should consider very carefully the full effect of its action. If this provision is put into force I suggest that the government at all times keep in mind the application of every possible control, statutory, regulatory or any other form, which will prevent the farmers who are already suffering sufficiently from suffering any additional handicap through the removal of competitive factors on one of our chief channels of trade.

The hon.
gentleman is all right and he is all wrong. He is right when he states that competition sets the freight rates. He has said that the competition on the great lakes will fix the rates in Vancouver.

Will be a factor in
fixing the rates.
All right. The rates in Vancouver will fix the rates on the great lakes.
Also a factor.

All right. As
soon as those rates are increased Vancouver will have more grain to ship. Last year I believe 120,000,000 bushels went through that port. Let them take another 120,000,000 bushels away from Fort William, and where would shipping on the lakes be?

Would it cost the
farmer a little more?

No, not a
cent. The farmers out there are shipping through Vancouver because it has the cheapest rate, and that competition will keep the lake rates down. As soon as the rates are raised, down will go the shipping.
Question.

I have one personal
observation to make, and I shall have finished. I come from a portion of Saskatchewan which I may describe as being on the shed. In other words, the rate to Vancouver is to us always the same as it is to the east, and my people are most interested because of the very point raised by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman). If you are going to make it possible to apply the maximum rate on the lakes you are going either to increase the shipments to Vancouver or increase the rates of shipment to Vancouver. There is no part of
western Canada, taking the meridian of Alberta and Saskatchewan, that is more vitally interested than that portion. I represent a part of that country, and I feel keenly on this matter.

When this matter was under discussion last year and the year before I stated that I had no harsh feelings towards the maritimes. As a matter of fact, I should like all Canadian produce that now goes via American Atlantic ports to go via our maritime ports. Even if the cost might be a trifle greater, in normal times I would not mind that extra cost if it were only say half or quarter of a cent. But when we are losing money on every blessed bushel we raise, every quarter of a cent means that much more loss to us. Last year we had magnificent crops in the district from which I come, yet we lost money. Wrell now, to ask us simply for sentimental reasons to lose a little more is something which is hard to swallow. I think too much of our maritime friends to quarrel with them, because I love that country,-its history, its peoiple, its tradition and the story of the early Acadians and British settling there. I am not going to quarrel with them now; do not make any mistake about it, because I do not feel that way. But I do feel that the government has been derelict in its duty in not settling this question about Canadian wheat going to the United Kingdom via Buffalo. What in the world was the sense of making an agreement here in this building without knowing what were to be the conditions under which grain was to enter the United Kingdom via Buffalo, whether it would be subject to the six cent duty or not? As a matter of fact, this government forgot all about it. I doubt if the question ever was raised in this building at the time the agreement was being made, and it was not until the hullabaloo was set up when the grain started to go via Buffalo that the government grew alarmed, and when the question was put up to them they were afraid to decide it-let the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) correct me if I am wrong. Had the question been settled at the outset whether our wheat could go via Buffalo and thereby escape the tax of six cents duty when it entered the United Kingdom, because it is a tax- there is no preference about it; it is a question of taxing or not taxing the grain when it enters British ports-there never would have been any trouble about it. But the government neglected to settle that question at the time of the bargain, and naturally it then became
Canada Shipping Act

a question whether the grain should go by our maritime ports and please the people of the maritimes or go via Buffalo and please the people of the west. The answer of the government and of the Minister of Trade and Commerce always was: This is a question for the British people to decide; it is their problem; we have nothing to do with it; it is they who gave the preference and so on, and so forth. But is that the case? It is not the case. It is just as much our problem as it is the problem of the British people. If the doctrine that it is the British people who have the say on this matter is correct, it is the British people who have the say on the bacon question, on the cattle question, on the tobacco question and on all the other questions that were dealt with at the Ottawa conference. There was every reason why there should have been a specific understanding at the time of the bargain. The question should never have been left open to cause differences amongst ourselves, because the maritime people naturally want our grain to go that way; we just as naturally do not want to pay any more by having it go that way, and to go that way would mean losing a little more money on every bushel we ship. I would like the Minister of Trade and Commerce to show cause why the government cannot settle this question with the British government. We have had the cattle quota question up recently, and that question should never have arisen, but it did arise and an agreement was come to about it and a quota decided upon. Why cannot this government sit in with the British people and decide whether or not our wheat can go via Buffalo direct to the United Kingdom without any handicap? It is their duty to do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: That was settled long ago.
It is not settled.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It certainly is.

It is settled on
the basis of every cargo on its merits.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
It has been settled, and
it has been explained a dozen times. Any cargo that has a through bill of lading, which is a perfectly proper and ordinary thing, is declared by the British authorities to be duty free.

That may be so,
but my understanding from the press, and my hon. friend should know better than I because all I had to go on was the press reports, is that every cargo is settled on its
(Mr. Motherwell.]
merits or demerits. Some go straight to the United. Kingdom and get the exemption from paying duty, and some do not. If the question is really settled I would like to know it because there would be no use in talking about it any more. If the minister would say that we cannot ship to the United Kingdom via Buffalo, that would end the matter. But we would then know where the responsibility lies. It would not be with the British government alone but with ours also; do not make any mistake about that.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of Marine
speechtext:
After having listened
to all this discussion, Mr. Chairman, I am sorry to say that the government cannot accept the amendment of my hon. friend from Lisgar (Mr. Brown). We are compiling in this statute all our existing laws concerning shipping, and we are simply asking the house to reaffirm in these sections what was adopted by the house at the last session, after careful study; this legislation was submitted by the government after strong representations had been made from all sides. We heard the Canadian mariners and the Canadian ship owners, who represented to us that when foreign ships were carrying grain or other goods on the great lakes from one Canadian port to another Canadian port our Canadian bottoms were tied up by hundreds along the shores of the great lakes and our Canadian mariners were standing idle on those . shores looking at foreign ships and foreign mariners carrying and handling our Canadian grain in foreign bottoms. All these questions were studied very carefully, and the house came to the conclusion at the last session that this coasting law should be adopted in order to put our Canadian mariners and our Canadian bottom owners on the same footing as the Americans.
This very question whether this law would bring an increase in transportation rates on the great lakes and thereby injure our western farmers was very carefully studied, and it was only after we had ascertained that we had a great surplus of Canadian bottoms on the great lakes, and that we were sure that there would be enough competition to protect the farmers of the west, that we came to the conclusion that we should introduce the legislation of last session. I do not see why Canadian bottoms could not carry Canadian grain at the same rate as foreign bottoms, if not at a lower rate. If we had thought for a moment that this legislation would have for its effect an injury to our farmers we would never have brought it down. There

Unemployment Relief
is no question, about that. But after very carefully studying the question we have come to the conclusion that we should embody in this bill the legislation which was very properly enacted at the last session.
That does not exempt the question from discussion.
